explainBack.question: Why might Muse send an email on your behalf without asking you at that moment, even though Meta advertises approval prompts?
explainBack.answer: Approvals are governed by a control outside the agent that matches each proposed action against the permission you already granted for that service. Permissions can be one-time, task- or session-limited, time-bounded or permanent, and previously allowed, read-only or low-risk actions may proceed without any fresh prompt. So if you earlier granted a lasting send permission, the control finds the action within scope and lets it through — the prompt only appears when the action falls outside what you already allowed.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: P005 (external control checks proposed action against the service's permission) and P006 (grant types, control chooses which to offer, previously allowed/low-risk actions proceed without interruption; prompts are design, not guarantee).
explainBack.assessment: Accurate: the article's mechanism fully supports this causal answer in ordinary language, including the reason prompts are not universal.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A reader wants Muse to watch her bank's website for a recurring subscription she suspects is double-billing her, and, if it finds one, to cancel it and request a refund through the bank's messaging system — a banking case the article never discusses.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, what access should she grant and what should she expect the system to do at each step?
unseenTransfer.answer: Per the article, each connected service is a separate decision, and read and action access can differ. Watching statements needs only read access, so she should grant read-only — the article says read-only actions may then proceed without repeated prompts. Cancelling and messaging the bank are actions that change her account, so she should grant those, if at all, as a one-time or task-limited permission rather than a permanent one; the outside control will check each proposed cancellation against that scope before it reaches the internet. Because the agent will make mistakes and prompt injection is open, she should verify the cancellation in the audit trail, and remember today's workspace does not block Meta's own access — sensitive financial data sits under the current, weaker privacy regime until the promised user-key version ships.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: P006 (scoped grants, read-only uninterrupted), P005 (external check per service), P007 (mistakes, prompt injection), P009 (read/action decision, audit trail), P008/P010 (current Meta access versus later promise).
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism resolves this novel banking scenario completely, including the risk posture — strong evidence the explanation transfers beyond its own examples.
